The enumerating shape the Swahili shilling established, for the two languages whose countries use several currencies with no shared name. Arabic's six countries use four words -- riyal in SA, pound in EG, dirham in AE and MA, dinar in JO and IQ -- and Arabic had no currency concept at all, which was the worst gap in the table. Russian's ruble already covers Russia and Belarus, whose currency is also a ruble; what it does not reach is Kazakhstan's tenge and Kyrgyzstan's som. No symbol row beside it, which every other currency has: a symbol row's respelling is blank where the text is a bare sign and junk where it is an abbreviation -- espeak read `ر.س · ج.م · د.إ · د.أ` as `rs dʒˈamm dʔ dʔ`, with the two dinars indistinguishable -- so the abbreviations ride in text_alt, which by design gets no IPA.

The unit gap `numbers-money.y-w-n` already accepts the shape of: a myriad-grouped number is one a Western reader cannot parse. India groups the same way and one step further up, and the Hindi pack stopped at `दस हज़ार`, so a reader who can count to ten thousand still could not read `₹5 लाख` on a price board -- which is how every Indian price above about a hundred thousand is written, along with the `1,00,000` digit grouping that goes with it, in text_alt. Its own cluster rather than `numbers-money.misc`: misc is the number line, so eighteen items of cluster decay would have made the balancer value a lakh at nothing.

One step above the lakh, and the step a price board reaches for real estate and for anything in the news. Arabic cannot print the numeral -- the validator refuses more than one digit in a right-to-left row, because the renderer would reverse them -- so `عشرة ملايين` is spelled out with the numeral in text_alt, which is the repair the five existing Arabic numeral rows took.
Israeli currency. One country, one currency, so it is a named row like the forint rather than the generic `local-currency` the six-country packs take.
The symbol as printed on a price. U+20AA, which no shipped face carried before this pack.
